name: Joseph of Arimathaea
charge: Going in boldly unto Pilate and craving the body; and not having consented to the counsel and deed of them
summary: Joseph of Arimathaea was an honourable counsellor who waited for the kingdom of God, a good man and a just, and he had not consented to the counsel and deed of the council he sat in (Mark 15:43; Luke 23:50-51). When the evening was come, because it was the preparation, he went in boldly to Pilate and craved the body. He took it down, wrapped it in clean linen, and laid it in his own new tomb hewn out of a rock, where no man had been laid before (Matthew 27:57-60).
offenseFull: He sat in the council that condemned Christ and did not consent to their counsel and deed (Luke 23:50-51). Not every man was let into that room, so the record is telling you he had standing among the Pharisees and was a follower of Christ at the same time. John says he was a disciple, but secretly, for fear of the Jews (John 19:38). That fear has a definition in the gospel: Christ had sent them out as sheep among wolves and told them to be wise as serpents and harmless as doves, and warned that men would deliver them up to the councils and scourge them in their synagogues (Matthew 10:16-18). Joseph was inside one of those councils. He is named with Nicodemus, who came to Christ by night and told him plainly that they knew he was a teacher come from God (John 3:1-2), and the two of them together are the proof that the rejection of Christ was the work of the elders, the chief priests and the scribes, and not of every man in the nation (Mark 8:31; John 8:31).

When the evening was come he went in boldly to Pilate and craved the body, which was the dangerous part of it (Mark 15:43). It takes position and standing to walk into that hall and ask a Roman governor for the corpse of a man his own court had just executed as a rebel, and to be heard. He used what he had, the way Esther used her place for the nation and Daniel used his. He bought fine linen, took the body down, wrapped it, laid it in a sepulchre hewn out of a rock, and rolled a stone to the door; Nicodemus came with him bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pound weight (Mark 15:46; John 19:39-40). The burial was made the same day, which is the custom written in the law: the body of a man hanged on a tree shall not remain all night, but shall be buried that day, that the land be not defiled (Deuteronomy 21:22-23). There is no waiting days over a body.
judgmentFull: The prophet had written that he would make his grave with the wicked and with the rich in his death (Isaiah 53:9). He was crucified between two malefactors, and then a rich man buried him in his own new sepulchre (Matthew 27:57-60). Joseph is how that word came to pass, and the passage names him as rich in the same sentence that names what he did with it.

The women who came with him out of Galilee followed after and beheld the sepulchre and how the body was laid, then returned and prepared spices and ointments, and rested the sabbath day according to the commandment (Luke 23:55-56). Their witness of the place is what makes the report bought from the watch worthless, because they knew exactly where the body had been put. Nothing is promised to Joseph in the text beyond the record itself. A counsellor who did not consent, who spent his standing, his linen and his own tomb on a body nobody else would claim, is named in all four gospels and set beside Nicodemus as proof that some of those men did change. The honour is in what he did, and in the word it fulfilled.

text.text: Joseph of Arimathea, an honourable counsellor, which also waited for the kingdom of God, came, and went in boldly unto Pilate, and craved the body of Jesus.
And, behold, there was a man named Joseph, a counsellor; and he was a good man, and a just:
(The same had not consented to the counsel and deed of them;) he was of Arimathea, a city of the Jews: who also himself waited for the kingdom of God.
When the even was come, there came a rich man of Arimathea, named Joseph, who also himself was Jesus’ disciple:
He went to Pilate, and begged the body of Jesus. Then Pilate commanded the body to be delivered.
And when Joseph had taken the body, he wrapped it in a clean linen cloth,
And laid it in his own new tomb, which he had hewn out in the rock: and he rolled a great stone to the door of the sepulchre, and departed.

And after this Joseph of Arimathea, being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, besought Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus: and Pilate gave him leave. He came therefore, and took the body of Jesus.
Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
But beware of men: for they will deliver you up to the councils, and they will scourge you in their synagogues;
And ye shall be brought before governors and kings for my sake, for a testimony against them and the Gentiles.
There was a man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews:
The same came to Jesus by night, and said unto him, Rabbi, we know that thou art a teacher come from God: for no man can do these miracles that thou doest, except God be with him.
And he began to teach them, that the Son of man must suffer many things, and be rejected of the elders, and of the chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and after three days rise again.
Then said Jesus to those Jews which believed on him, If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed;
And he bought fine linen, and took him down, and wrapped him in the linen, and laid him in a sepulchre which was hewn out of a rock, and rolled a stone unto the door of the sepulchre.
And there came also Nicodemus, which at the first came to Jesus by night, and brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about an hundred pound weight.
Then took they the body of Jesus, and wound it in linen clothes with the spices, as the manner of the Jews is to bury.
And if a man have committed a sin worthy of death, and he be to be put to death, and thou hang him on a tree:

His body shall not remain all night upon the tree, but thou shalt in any wise bury him that day; (for he that is hanged is accursed of God;) that thy land be not defiled, which the Lord thy God giveth thee for an inheritance.
And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death; because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.
And the women also, which came with him from Galilee, followed after, and beheld the sepulchre, and how his body was laid.
And they returned, and prepared spices and ointments; and rested the sabbath day according to the commandment.

And after this Joseph of Arimathea, being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, besought Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus: and Pilate gave him leave. He came therefore, and took the body of Jesus.
And there came also Nicodemus, which at the first came to Jesus by night, and brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about an hundred pound weight.
Then took they the body of Jesus, and wound it in linen clothes with the spices, as the manner of the Jews is to bury.
Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden; and in the garden a new sepulchre, wherein was never man yet laid.
There laid they Jesus therefore because of the Jews’ preparation day; for the sepulchre was nigh at hand.
